text: {"score":3,"justification":"Numbers are largely grounded in the card and tool outputs, and the case is well-structured with relevant citations and a cautious 'needs human chart review'. But there are internal contradictions and a headline mismatch that would mislead an investigator, and the next steps contain a conflicting instruction about the overpayment estimate.","problems":["Headline says '99215 billed on 24% of visits for patients with no chronic conditions (peers 2.2%)' — card gives 24.4% vs 2.2% for 0 conditions, OK, but later rationale says 84% of 99215s were on 0 or 1 conditions; headline 'z_adj 26.5' is jargon not in card.","Headline '7 of 30 random charts support a lower level' mixes the all-code figure with the 99215 rule (4 of 8, 50%) used as the basis; the leaning rests on only 8 documented 99215 claims, a small sample whose thinness is not flagged.","Rationale states 'Notes do not look inflated' yet next step says 43% of notes address fewer problems than their level implies and asks for audit trail, which is contradictory; also 'No audit trail was received' is not supported by tool output shown (only MISSING_RESULTS deficiency noted).","Next step says to review the random sample 'before any overpayment estimate; do not extrapolate from a targeted sample', but the rationale already presents a random-sample overpayment estimate ($11,492) and the sample was random, so the guidance is confusing.","The MISSING_RESULTS deficiency is not mentioned; the '2 of 18 notes with data reviewed but no lab line' is stated without explaining relevance.","Example claims cited for low complexity (heart failure, atrial fibrillation) are chronic serious conditions, which weakens them as support for 'low complexity'; example claims are from code-formatted text, selected without a high-complexity counterexample (5 high-complexity 99215s exist) and supported 99215s are omitted."]}
